<meta>continues from previous page: He shall not be made to pay if it is seized by the King, by an act of God, or by thieves.</meta>
The deposit <term>upanidhi</term> is not to be paid for by the person with whom it was placed if it is taken or destroyed by the King, by an act of God—such as by water or similar means—or by thieves. That property belongs to the owner <term>dhanin</term> alone if the destruction does not occur through deceit <term>jihma</term> <gloss>fraudulent act</gloss>. As **Narada** says: "That which is destroyed together with the property of the recipient <note>meaning the recipient's own goods destroyed alongside the deposit</note> is destroyed; that is the owner's loss. The same applies to losses by fate <note>act of God</note> or the King, provided it was not caused by deceit."

He states an exception to this:

### 66. If there is a delay when it has been requested, he shall be made to pay [the value] and an equal amount as a fine.

If the owner requests or demands the return of the item and the recipient does not give it back, then, even if a loss <term>bhreṣa</term> occurs later by the King or others, the recipient must pay the value of the property to the owner and a fine of an equal amount to the King. 66.

He states the penalty for one who uses the deposit:

### He who makes use of it at will shall be fined and forced to pay it back along with interest.

One who uses or trades with a deposited item for profit, such as by investment, without the owner's permission, shall be fined according to the extent of the use and the profit generated. Furthermore, he shall be made to pay the owner the deposit along with interest if he used it, or along with the profit if he traded with it. The measure of the interest is stated by **Katyayana**: "If one does not return a deposit, the remaining interest, a purchase, or a sale when requested, it increases by five percent per month." This applies to when the item has been consumed. For items lost through negligence <term>upekṣā</term> <gloss>ignoring/neglecting</gloss>, a specific distinction is shown by the same author: "For consumed items, he shall be made to pay with interest; for neglected items, he shall be made to pay an equal amount; for items lost through ignorance, he shall be made to pay slightly less." "Slightly less" means reduced by one-fourth.

He extends these rules for the deposit to requested items and others:

### 67. This rule applies to requested items, those transferred for delivery, bailments, and deposits.

An item such as a garment or ornament borrowed for a festival or similar occasion is a <term>yācita</term> <gloss>requested item</gloss>. That which is placed in the hands of one person with the instruction to hand it over to the owner later is <term>anvāhita</term> <gloss>transferred for delivery</gloss>. A <term>nyāsa</term> <gloss>bailment</gloss> is an item placed in the custody of a household member without the householder's knowledge, with the intention that it be delivered to the householder later. A <term>nikṣepa</term> <gloss>deposit</gloss> is a handing over in the presence [of the owner]. The word "etc." includes gold or similar materials given to a goldsmith for the manufacture of bracelets and the like, as well as "counter-deposits" <term>pratinyāsa</term>, where, out of mutual need, one party says, "You must protect this of mine," and the other says, "I will protect this of yours." As **Narada** says: "This very rule is seen to apply to requested items, transferred items, etc., to craftsmanship, deposits, bailments, and counter-deposits." In all these cases, such as requested items and those transferred for delivery, this rule—the procedure for return and so on—should be understood to be the same as that for the deposit. 67.

->Thus ends the Section on Deposits.<-

---

<margin>
1. "That should be" is the reading in version B; "that should be deceitful" is another reading. 2. "Uses it" (version B); "enjoys the fruits" (version C). 3. "Being requested" (version C). 4. "In the case of neglect, 'you this...'" (version B).
</margin>

<summary>This section defines the liability of a bailee for various forms of property transfer, including requested items and bailments, establishing that unauthorized use or failure to return items upon request incurs fines and interest, with specific penalties for consumption or neglect.</summary>
